description: We are a group of minds that are intrigued about everything from coding to dreams and enjoy bringing crazy ideas to life through prototyping. Participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge is the best opportunity to work together, consume too much caffeine, and do something useful. And we are short on VRAM.
summary: The SPHEREx Temporal Subtraction & Anomaly Engine is a web tool that helps astronomers and curious people find moving or changing objects in NASA’s SPHEREx telescope data, which scans the entire sky every six months in infrared light. The core idea is simple: take two images of the same patch of sky from different dates, subtract one from the other, and anything that moved or changed brightness will pop out as a bright or dark blob in the result, a trick called difference imaging that is basically how Pluto was discovered back in 1930. The tricky parts are that the images come buried inside huge 65 MB files on NASA’s servers (so the tool fetches only tiny postage-stamp cutouts instead), the sky background changes between visits because of dust in our solar system (so it gets subtracted out before comparing), and the two images do not line up pixel-for-pixel because the telescope was rotated differently each time (so they get mathematically re-aligned first). Once all that is handled, the tool scores every suspicious pixel by how statistically significant it is, converts the pixel coordinates back into real sky coordinates, and displays everything in a browser-based dashboard where you can blink between the two epochs, inspect a color-coded difference map, and download a ranked table of candidate discoveries, all without any coding or telescope expertise required.
details: The SPHEREx Temporal Subtraction & Anomaly Engine is a full-stack web application designed to help discover moving celestial bodies, such as brown dwarfs and asteroids, as well as variable stars from NASA's near-infrared sky surveys. The platform automates the heavy astrophysics workflow by querying NASA's IRSA TAP database for targeted Multi-Extension FITS cutouts, cleaning zodiacal dust, and utilizing Astropy WCS interpolation to align multi-epoch observations. By subtracting baseline reference images from follow-up frames, stationary background stars cancel out while moving objects leave distinct dipole signatures that are automatically detected and logged into an interactive anomaly table with CSV export.
